reason: The text demonstrates that Yahweh does show empathy and mercy toward the people, not merely judgment. Although God initially threatens to destroy the people and replace them with a nation from Moses (Numbers 14:11-12), Moses intercedes on their behalf. God then explicitly grants forgiveness (וַיֹּ֣אמֶר יְהוָ֔ה סָלַ֖חְתִּי - 'And the Lord said, I have forgiven'), revealing His character as 'slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love' (יְהוָ֗ה אֶ֤רֶךְ אַפַּ֙יִם֙ וְרַב־ חֶ֔סֶד). While the unfaithful generation faces consequences in the wilderness, God promises their children will inherit the land (וּ֠בְנֵיכֶם יִהְי֨וּ רֹעִ֤ים בַּמִּדְבָּר), indicating concern for the people's future. The distinction Yahweh makes is based on faith rather than social status—Caleb and Joshua are favored for their trust, not because they are 'leaders.' God's forgiveness and inheritance promise to the next generation contradict the claim that He lacks empathy for the people.
